I did this on my home network with a pfSense firewall/server. I have the office LAN on 10.64.0.0/24, the house LAN on 10.64.1.0/24, the office DMZ on 10.64.2.0/24, phones are 192.168.14.0/24 (bought used PoE switch... got lazy), and the guest network is 10.64.3.0/24. I have configured the firewall to allow certain traffic to pass between subnets. My media server is on the house subnet but traffic is allowed to pass from the office and guest network to it (but only specific ports and protocols, and only to that IP), same with the internal DNS server which resides on the office LAN. Each subnet has its own public IP just because it seemed easier that way. The advantage to this is the ability to have different security levels on each subnet and the added protection of things such as Snort and real time filtering of malicious traffic.

Granted, that's probably quite a bit more horsepower than you have available for a router(s), but it's not like you can't pick up a cheap PC to do the same thing with, and you'll probably get better throughput than with the SOHO routers you have now.

For the "protection" of media stuff, I'd recommend using nothing more complex than different user accounts on the media side. The user account that my tv's and game systems use to access the media server only has read/traverse permission on the server side.

The problem with using lower end routers for network segregation is that they often have both gaping security issues, as well as just not being up to the task to handling larger amounts of traffic. Although I like the Asus routers (moreso being based on dd-wrt), I don't think they're up to serious use, especially when you have a more complex network, and/or higher security requirements.
